subject: pigeonKnight
pitch:
Category: Humanoid character.
Subject: pigeon in knight's armour.
Style: medieval manuscript marginalia.
reasoning:
I'm picturing a bipedal pigeon standing upright in knight's armor, rendered in the flat colors, gold leaf, and ink outlines of medieval manuscript marginalia, and planning how to build this as a single TypeScript module.

I'm settling on a palette of parchment cream, vermilion, lapis, gold, and ink brown-black, with the armor done in gold leaf and lapis accents over a heraldic surcoat bearing a pigeon-and-crumbs emblem. I'm roughing out the proportions now: a stylized chunky humanoid about 1.2 meters tall, with short pink-vermilion legs ending in bird feet, hips around y=0.52, and a plump breast-chest fitted with a gold breastplate.

Now I'm continuing the spine chain up through the chest to the neck base, then shaping the head as a round pigeon face with a beak, topped by an open-faced helmet so the eyes and beak stay visible, with a mail aventail at the neck and a red-and-blue feather plume on top.

Then I'm thinking through the arms, using folded pigeon wings as the limb structure with shoulder-elbow-wrist joints, ending in a fan of 3-4 primary feathers acting as fingers, keeping the signature grey-blue plumage with dark wing bars, armored with pauldrons and vambraces, and holding a sword in one wing-hand and a shield in the other.

Now I'm settling on an A-pose with arms angled outward about 40°, sword held upright at the right wrist and shield strapped to the left forearm, plus a fanned pigeon tail behind the hips built from extruded feather shapes.

For the surcoat, I'm planning a tabard over the torso using loft/frustum boxes front and back with a heraldic lapis-and-gold emblem — a dove holding a bread crust flanked by three gold bezants — finished with a flared skirt, a buckled belt, and marginalia-style gold rivets and floral vine trim.

I'm staying true to the brief by skipping extras like a snail or parchment base that aren't named, keeping just sword and shield. Now I'm settling on a flat color palette: parchment, ink, vermillion, lapis, gold, dark gold, verdigris green, and pigeon grey.

For the pigeon's neck I want that iridescent green-purple sheen, and for the armour I'll use a custom paint with hammered mottle and warm-cool countershading rather than flat silver.

Starting to set up the TypeScript imports and builder structure...

I'm checking whether the glow kit is importable for small gold accents, like luminous manuscript leaf on rivets, though I'm wary of overusing it since the material needs to stay simple.

Now I'm working out the leg dimensions and joint placements—hip positions, foot targets, thigh and shin lengths—checking that the limb reach roughly matches the hip-to-foot height, with a slight knee bend forward for a humanoid armored stance.

I'm setting up the leg chains parented to the hips joint, naming each segment (hip, knee, ankle) so the limb function produces the right tip joint, and figuring out the side naming convention so positive X corresponds to the model's left leg.

For the legs themselves, I want thin pink-red pigeon limbs partially covered by armour—cuisse and poleyn plating on the thigh and knee, with a greave on the upper shin, leaving the lower tarsus bare and pink like a real pigeon's leg.

Figuring out the leg sweep with varying radius...

Actually a cleaner approach: split into separate sweeps rather than one tube with abrupt radius changes — a thigh sweep tapering in steel, a greave sweep tapering with gold trim, then a pink tarsus sweep, with a gold poleyn sphere at the knee joint and gold cuff rings as torus shapes. I'm now sketching a helper function to build these arm/leg tubes from a chain with given from/to ranges.

Now I'm working out the legs as polyline paths built from an array of joint points, then adding feet: an ankle joint with toe capsules radiating forward and backward (three front toes plus one hind toe) as thin capsule shapes attached to the ankle bone, each toe tipped with its own joint.

I'm deciding to keep bare clawed feet rather than hiding them under armor, maybe adding a small gold heel spur for flavor, and noting the toe caps as the lowest point of the model.

Now I'm placing the toe capsules so their rounded ends touch the ground plane, positioning the forward toes sloping down from the ankle and adding a hind toe behind it, then checking that the tarsus joint and tube sit above the floor without clipping. Next I start thinking about the torso shape for the pigeon body.

Then I plan the spine chain as a sequence of joints rising from the hip up through the chest, defining a loft path with named segments for spine and chest sections, parented to the hips, followed by a short neck chain of two joints leading up toward the head position.

I'm sizing the overall figure as a chibi pigeon-knight around 1.3m tall, with the head sitting atop the neck and a plume extending higher still. For the body, I'm defining loft stations along the spine with widths and depths that puff out at the belly for that rounded pigeon-breast silhouette, narrowing toward the hips and chest, using the spine chain as the loft's bone path with the default frame orientation giving width along x and depth along z.

Now I'm figuring out how the knight's armor layers over the pigeon body—the feathered torso showing mainly at the neck as an iridescent gorget, with a breastplate loft slightly larger than the body underneath, then a tabard hanging as front and back panels from the shoulders. I'm realizing a flat plane panel won't conform to the curved belly, so I need a better approach for shaping the cuirass itself.

I'm deciding to color the cuirass loft with a quartered lapis-and-gold cloth pattern and apply a heraldic emblem decal onto the chest surface. Below the belt I'm adding a flared lathe skirt with a dagged scalloped hem made from alternating small cone spikes in vermilion and lapis for a proper medieval look.

Checking the leg placement against the skirt geometry, the hem radius comfortably clears the thighs so the legs read naturally beneath the fabric, with the hem landing around upper-thigh height and knees peeking just below. For the torso design, I'm settling on a lapis surcoat worn over a steel cuirass with visible pauldrons, a gorget, and a plated belt with gold studs for added detail and contrast.

Writing emblem SVG path...

Still designing the shield geometry...

Still deciding on the heraldry — settling on a lapis field with a parchment chevron and gold bezants above it as the simplest readable composition.

Now I'm working out how the shield should be mounted on the left forearm so it faces forward outward rather than showing just its edge in the front view, angling the shield's normal slightly outward from a position around the left wrist/forearm.

I also need to nail down the extrusion directions for the shield outline — since the model faces +Z, its left side corresponds to +X, so from a viewer's perspective looking at the front, the model's left arm appears on the viewer's right side of the screen, which determines how I orient the x and y extrude axes for the shield shape.

For the shield itself I'll keep it facing front with no tilt, positioning it over the left forearm so it sits in front of the arm (partially obscuring it) without blocking the face, sized around 0.34 wide by 0.42 tall.

Now I'm working out the arm geometry: shoulder at roughly (0.25,0.97,0), with the upper arm angling outward about 35° to an elbow near (0.37,0.81,0), then the forearm continuing to a wrist around (0.47,0.64,0.04), with the hand hanging down and out from there.

I'm reconsidering the shield placement though, since putting it directly over the forearm would hide too much of the arm. Instead I'll keep the arm in A-pose and center the shield lower, just below the elbow, around (0.45, 0.62, 0.12) with dimensions roughly 0.3 wide by 0.4 tall.

But that still obscures the wrist and hand feathers behind it, so I'll finalize the shield's position more toward the outside of the forearm, angled, at around (0.36, 0.62, 0.16) with height 0.44, letting the wing feathers fan out visibly past its edge.

I'll go with a wider A-pose at about 48°, letting the shield mostly cover the forearm while the hand/wrist peek out at x≈0.55 and the elbow stays visible above the shield's top edge. For the right arm holding the sword, I'm setting the shoulder at (-0.25, 0.97) and working out the elbow position next.

For the sword arm, I'll angle the wrist slightly outward from the elbow, with the blade pointing mostly upward and a touch forward so its tip clears the head comfortably. I'll wrap the feather-fan "hand" around the grip near the wrist, with some primaries curling forward over the hilt to sell the idea of it gripping the sword, crossguard sitting just above.

For the wing feathers, I'm designing a reusable feather-building function that creates a joint at the wrist with an aim direction, then extrudes a tapered feather outline along that direction to form each primary digit.

Checking the dir=(0,-1,0) case confirms x points in -X, which is fine since the outline is symmetric anyway. Now I'm defining the feather outline as a symmetric set of points tapering from a wide base to a sharp tip, using smoothing for a natural curve.

Extruding the feather shape with a small thickness and setting up a paint function that colors it grey with a darker tip band based on position along its length, essentially a gradient closure keyed to each feather's length. I'm weighing the texture-sheet cost of so many painted parts against using flat colors instead, but decide the gradient paint is worth it for realism.

I'm also considering an alternative approach: drawing feathers as SVG card textures with ink outlines, barb lines, and quill details, placed on double-sided quads oriented along bone frames — this could work well for wing, tail, and plume feathers where cards naturally face along the flow direction of each joint.

I need to work out the flow direction carefully so the feather drawing reads correctly from the viewer's side rather than appearing mirrored or backwards.

Each feather card is just four cheap triangles carrying painted texture detail, tinted with greys, and double-sided so they shade correctly using the frame's facing axis as the lighting normal—meaning feathers pointing downward will appear darker since they're lit as an underside.

I'm reconsidering this: maybe the frame should face outward-forward instead, with lean angling toward the flow direction so angled feathers tip laterally rather than straight back along the axis.

I realize with flow=+X and width=axis×flow, the card ends up edge-on to the viewer instead of facing them — the face normal lands in the wrong plane. I want the card to face Z, so flow should point along ±Z instead, meaning I need to rethink which axis handles the lean versus which handles spin.

Maybe I should pick a frame axis that's tilted at some angle rather than straight up, blending toward the flow direction, and let lean do the tipping work — though that still complicates how the card plane ends up oriented relative to the light source.

Actually cards might not be the right primitive for feathers at all — maybe I should reconsider using extrude with textures instead, since paints apply to sweeps, lofts, extrudes, lathes, membranes and slabs, letting me build my own mapped geometry.

I'll pass `up: [0,0,1]` to keep the plane's normal facing forward regardless of bone direction, so down-pointing and sideways feathers both stay visible. Now writing the plank helper function...

I'll use alpha-tested textures to carve the feather silhouette, varying designs across grey wing feathers with dark tips, tail feathers, and vermilion plume feathers for visual variety. For the arms, I'm planning layered feather cards for the wing coverts alongside separate armor pieces—vambrace, rerebrace, and couter—to cover the forearm, upper arm, and elbow.

I've worked out a readable pigeon-wing look: pauldron and rerebrace cover the upper arm, a partial vambrace wraps the forearm, and five secondary feather planes hang down from the underside of the forearm toward the wrist, fanning slightly, with primaries appearing at the hand—this gives the dark wing-bar silhouette I want. Time to start coding; I'm organizing the build into a component list starting with setup, palette, and text elements.

Now I'm planning the full build order: skeleton bones for hips, spine, neck, head, jaw, legs, arms, and tail; the pigeon's body loft with neck sweep and gorget; head details including skull, cheek, beak halves, cere bump, eye decals, and helm; armour pieces (cuirass, belt, skirt, pauldrons, vambraces, greaves, gorget); wing feathers; tail fan with chain bones; plus sword, shield, plume, and emblem decals. I'm setting height constants, placing the hips around y=0.55 and the head center near y=1.28, with the head module sized to one scale unit.

Working out the head center position precisely at (0, 1.27, 0.10) with a skull sphere radius around 0.13 for a cute stylized look, and figuring out the neck geometry running from the body up to the head joint, aiming the head slightly forward and upward. I'm deciding to position head features using absolute offsets from the head center rather than local bone-relative axes to keep things simple, and starting to define the skull sphere geometry with grayish-lilac pigeon coloring plus a helper function for coordinate placement.

Now I'm shaping the beak as a tapered sweep from base to tip with narrowing radius profile, choosing a dark horn-brown color for realism with a pale cere lump at the base, and placing a jaw joint near the beak's root.

Checking the beak overlap at root and tip to make sure it looks like a closed mouth rather than gapped or crossed.

Now I'm setting up the beak as a swept shape along a short path with radii controlling width and height per segment. For the eyes, I'm placing orange pigeon-style iris decals on the sides of the skull near the front, positioned at roughly ±55° azimuth and 8° elevation.

Adding bare-skin eyering details...

I need to work out the mirroring carefully: since the model's left eye at +X appears on the viewer's right, its inner corner toward the beak is actually on the viewer's left side. The determined brow should slope downward toward center, so I'm tracing the lid line going from high on the outer side down toward the inner corner.

Since I'm drawing this specifically as the left eye, the right eye needs the mirror flag flipped relative to what the kit example used. I'll also account for the eye sitting on a curved skull surface, viewed at roughly 48° azimuth and 8° elevation, with a slightly larger decal size, and I need to double check how the "dir" parameter determines which way the drawing faces.

Now I'm sketching out the pigeon-style bascinet helm: a lathed dome centered just above the skull center with a radius a bit larger than the skull itself, defining the cross-section profile points that sweep from the base up to the crown to give it thickness and shape, open at the face. I'm wary that if the rim sits too low it'll cover the eyes, so I need to tune the rim height carefully.

I'm positioning the dome's rim just above eye level, and planning an aventail—a mail neck guard—as a lathed frustum shape flaring around the neck below the helm's back and sides. For the mail texture I'm considering a custom procedural paint function that renders a ring pattern using a grid of small circles with darker borders to mimic chainmail.

I'm deciding against a nasal bar in front of the face since the eyes sit on the sides and nothing should block the beak area, opting instead for a plain gold brow band torus across the forehead.

I'll add a gold crest ridge running front-to-back along the dome and a socket tube at the top-back to hold a plume made of several fanned vermilion feather planes with ink outlines, arranged leaning upward and backward from the holder.

For the neck, I want an iridescent pigeon-feather effect — mixing a teal-green and purple shimmer color based on the surface normal and some noise, shifting with the x-direction of the normal to create that natural sheen.

I'm adding a steel gorget ring at the base of the neck with gold trim, leaving the iridescent feathers visible just above it. For the torso, since the cuirass covers most of the body, I'll skip a separate feathered body mesh and let the surcoat suggest the pigeon's puffed-out breast instead.

I'll keep the torso as the surcoat for a strong heraldic color mass of lapis, vermilion, and gold, reserving steel for the pauldrons, gorget, vambraces, greaves, helm, and belt plate rather than a separate breastplate.

For the surcoat I'm thinking lapis cloth with a gold diaper pattern, like a manuscript background — a diamond lattice with thin gold lines and dots at the intersections, computed using diagonal coordinate combinations and picking the dominant face (front vs. side) based on surface normal direction so it reads correctly on a round torso. I'm also considering adding a vertical vermilion band down the front for a "per pale" heraldic division.

Actually I like splitting the coat left/right: one side lapis, the other vermilion, like a classic per-pale heraldic design, with the gold diaper lattice overlaid on both sides and a dove roundel decal centered on the chest over the dividing line. I'll extend that same x-sign color split to the skirt for continuity, and color the skirt's dag cones individually by which side of the center line they fall on, keeping the shield placement independent of this scheme. Since the wings serve as arms, there's no need for separate sleeves.

Computing dag placement around the hem...

Defining the skirt's radial profile...

Hem sits at y=0.42 with dags tapering down to 0.36, sized as small triangular flaps spaced around the circumference, colored the same as the surcoat paint. Now I'm sketching the belt as a swept loop around the torso at y=0.64 with a tapered radius for a steel/gold band.

For the buckle plate, I'm defining a gold loop path on the torso surface and sweeping a flattened box section around it, though I'm uncertain whether the orientation (binormal vs normal) will correctly align the flat side of the band against the body on a closed horizontal loop.

Deciding to just use a simple circular tube for the belt cord instead, paired with a buckle piece, going for a knight's chain-belt look rather than risking a twisted ribbon.

Now I'm laying out the torso loft stations with width, depth, and z-center values at each height, building the puffed chest/belly profile that tapers back in near the shoulders.

Checking that the shoulder joints and pauldron spheres sit just outside the torso's halfwidth so they don't clip, confirming the pivot positions look right.

Working out the loft and sweep function signatures -- figuring out whether `bone` expects a chain or an array of chains and joints, and setting up the spine chain path with named joints at increasing heights and z-offsets to drive the torso's curvature.

Now continuing to the neck chain: plotting its three points from the chest up to the head, parenting it to the end of the spine chain, and defining the head and jaw joints with their own positions and hinge directions. Then setting up the sweep radii for the neck shape.

Checking overall proportions next: skull center sits above the head joint with roughly 0.125 radius, so top of skull lands near 1.395m, and with the helm and plume it pushes total height to about 1.65m -- more human-scaled than I expected for a pigeon knight, so I'm reconsidering whether a stylized/chibi proportion (legs ~0.55, torso to 1.05, head 0.25, totaling ~1.4m without the plume) fits better.

Now I'm setting up the arm chain from shoulder to elbow to wrist, parented off the chest joint, with the wrist as the tip joint aimed along the final tangent. I'm layering sweeps for this: a thin grey feathered arm underneath, then steel armor pieces (rerebrace and vambrace) with tapering radii and a gold cuff ring, plus hanging secondary feather planes for visible pigeon coverts between the plates.

For the hand, I'm fanning four primary feather digits off the wrist tip, rotating the forearm direction vector around the Z axis at angles like -25°, -8°, 10°, and 28° to spread them naturally.

Now I'm mirroring that fan for the right side by flipping the rotation sign, placing each primary joint at the wrist with its own feather plane, and figuring out how the sword grip and shield strap interact with the hanging feathers -- accepting some overlap since the shield will hide the left side anyway. I'm also considering whether to add rows of covert feathers on the upper arm but may skip that for simplicity.

The real identity marker is the pigeon's two dark wing bars, so I'm designing the feather SVG with a grey base fill, a pair of ink-dark stripes near the tip, a rachis line, and hatch marks for barbs. For the tail, I'm building a short two-joint chain from the rump that fans out into nine feather planes angled backward and down, oriented so their faces catch the light correctly, spanning roughly eighty degrees of azimuth behind the hips.

I'm now checking the geometry carefully since the tail feathers risk poking through the surcoat's skirt -- working out the skirt's flare radius at different heights and comparing it against where the downward-angled tail feathers would sit, to make sure the feathers clear the fabric surface rather than intersecting it.

Tail tip ends around y 0.6. I'll give the tail a dark terminal band with ink outlines for texture. Setting up a two-joint tail chain parented to the hips, running from the root point back and down to the tip for a drooping fan shape.

Now I'm attaching feathers alternately along the two tail bones, plus a sweep for a rump feather lump. For the sword, I'm rigging it to the right wrist as a rigid attachment, building the grip, gold crossguard and pommel, and a steel blade using an extrusion along a tilted axis so it angles slightly outward and up.

I'm figuring out the blade's fuller groove by painting a thinner darker strip down its center, and computing the correct perpendicular directions so the blade's thickness and width axes align properly with its tilt.

For inscription, I'm considering adding a thin textured plane in front of the blade with gold runic lettering like "SPES·PAX," possibly rotated vertically via SVG text transforms, rather than trying to decal directly onto the extruded geometry.

Now I'm working out the sword's placement relative to the right wrist, calculating grip, guard, and blade positions along the arm's direction vector so the blade tip lands near the head without overlap, and checking whether the blade geometry might intersect the forearm segment.

I'm also planning a steel wrist cuff for the sword hand, and thinking through the shield placement on the left, positioning its center and edge relative to the left wrist and primaries so it sits visibly in front without obscuring the hand.

Checking the shield against the torso geometry now, I realize the shield depth would intersect the chest if placed too close, so I'm shifting its x and z center outward and forward, verifying the new position clears the torso half-width and the shoulder pauldron while keeping it near the forearm.

Since the gap between forearm and shield is small but present, I'll bridge it with two strap boxes acting as "enarmes" (arm straps), then slightly rotate the shield around the Y axis so its outer edge angles backward toward the arm for a more natural fit. I'm working out the rotated edge and normal vectors to get the shield's facing direction correct after this yaw adjustment.

Now I'm defining the heater shield's outline coordinates -- a classic pointed shape about 0.34m wide and 0.46m tall, with sharp top corners and a smooth curve down to the tip.

I'm positioning the shield at the body so its tip clears the floor and its top sits just above the elbow joint. Then I'll create the shield's plane geometry for applying the face artwork.

For the heater shield shape itself, I'll build an extruded border slightly larger than the SVG outline, then overlay a smaller plane with the matching heater-shaped path texture centered over it.

I need the front face positioned at thickness/2, so 0.015 shifted to 0.0165, while using `frame: shield` to inherit orientation but overriding position with an explicit `at:` value.

For the shield rim boss, I'm thinking of a central gold hemisphere boss, possibly using a lathe operation, with a dove-roundel emblem rendered directly as the SVG shape.

Now I'm sketching the SVG decoration scheme: a lapis field with a gold chevron and three gold bezants above it, the chevron edged in vermilion with gold trim. I'm also drafting the texture list needed—pigeon eye, wing feather bars, tail feather, plume feather, shield face, dove roundel chest emblem, sword inscription, and possibly helm band and surcoat hem trims.

I'm settling on a back-of-torso decal: a vermilion-gold vine scroll with leaves in a lozenge, placed high enough on the upper back to avoid being covered by the tail. I'm also considering a small painted cross detail on the helm for extra character.

Thinking through collar and body details, I decide to skip the feathered mantling collar idea for time, and skip a scalloped cape too. For the legs, I'm working out that the thighs stay hidden under the skirt while the cuisse armor sweeps from the hip down to roughly the mid-thigh point.

Checking the limb helper function's signature, I confirm it takes a root point, target point, segment lengths, and bend directions, returning the chain of joint positions. I'm verifying the geometry works out: with hip at y=0.55 and foot near the ground, the two 0.27-length segments comfortably span the ~0.5 distance, so the knee bends forward slightly to satisfy the triangle inequality.

I'm now thinking through how to layer the leg visuals — bare skin below the knee, a greave (armor piece) covering part of the shin, and the tarsus/ankle region in pink, picking rough t-value ranges along the limb spline for where each material should start and stop.

For the upper leg, I'm setting up a sweep from hip to knee for the cuisse armor, then designing a gold knee cop (poleyn) as a flattened sphere with an optional small forward spike for a gothic armor look, attached to the knee joint.

Skipping sabatons since the feet stay bare with spurs. For the shoulders, I'm planning layered pauldron lames using nested lathe domes with an outward-tilted axis, topped with a gold ridge ring and a decorative spike knob on each side, plus a small spiked sphere for the elbow couter, and sweeps for the vambrace and rerebrace with tapering steel radii along the forearm and upper arm.

For gold trim at the cuffs, I'm writing a helper that builds a ring of points around the limb and sweeps a closed catmull curve through them to form a thin decorative band, making sure the ring radius is slightly larger than the limb and that the sweep inherits the correct bone. Now I'm sketching out a steel paint function with a mottled base pattern.

I'm reconsidering the overall art direction toward a manuscript-style flat illustration with ink outlines, which points me toward reusing the toon kit's cel shading for both cloth and steel to get that hard two-tone flat look rather than standard smooth lighting. I'm planning to use inkLines to create rim outlines on key silhouette edges — helm, torso, pauldrons, limbs — since that function draws dark lines where surface normals are perpendicular to a chosen view axis, mimicking hand-inked contour lines on spherical and cylindrical shapes. I'm setting up a small helper function to wrap a color with both cel shading and optional ink outlines so I can apply this consistently across the figure's parts.

Still writing styles...

For the tail feather I'll give it a dark band near the tip with a pale grey edge for that pigeon look, keeping the base lilac-grey. Then for the plume feather I'm setting up a curved vermilion shape with a white stripe and ink outline on a taller viewbox.
